solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Top politician going to European film debut

parts.note: a premier is a prime minister, the leading politician
E is the standard abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A senior politician turns up at the opening night of a European movie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going to' simply means the second piece is attached to the first, giving PREMIERE.
explanation.definitionFit: A premiere is the first public screening of a movie, its opening night before general release.

clue.text: Lustre going off in sequel

indicators.note: food going off has spoiled and changed state, so these letters break down into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A shine fades over the course of a follow-up film or book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sequel' suggests a film follow-up, but here it is used in its older sense of a consequence.
explanation.definitionFit: A sequel can mean something that follows as a consequence, which is exactly what an outcome or upshot is.

clue.text: Oral statement of offender on Monday is spicy stuff

indicators.note: an oral statement is something spoken out, so what follows is to be heard rather than read

parts.note: a sinner is an offender, and the first part of the spice is pronounced the same way
Mon is the usual abbreviation for Monday

explanation.surface: A wrongdoer's confession made at the start of the week turns out to be hot stuff.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the first piece is a sound-alike: SINNER said aloud gives the opening of CINNAMON, and the weekday abbreviation is added in plain spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Cinnamon is a common warming spice made from tree bark, so it is an example of spicy stuff.

clue.text: Create market that's failing regularly?

indicators.note: something failing at regular intervals drops out every so often, so letters vanish at a fixed spacing

parts.note: every third letter is dropped, losing the third and sixth

explanation.surface: Someone is told to set up a trading place that keeps going under now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropping every third letter of the six-letter word removes R and T, leaving MAKE.
explanation.definitionFit: To make something is to bring it into being, a plain synonym for create or produce.

clue.text: Looks up to take in introduction of theatrical Hollywood star

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading the letters from bottom to top, backwards
taking something in means admitting it inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: to peer is to look closely, so 'looks' gives the verb form

indicators.note: an introduction comes at the very start, so only the opening letter is wanted

parts.note: first letter of theatrical

explanation.surface: Someone admires a big-screen actress, taking in her stage presence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Looks up' reads as admiring someone, but 'up' tells you to reverse the verb, then T goes in after the first letter. Meryl Streep is the much-awarded American film actress.
explanation.definitionFit: Meryl Streep is a famous American screen actress, so she is an example of a Hollywood star.

clue.text: Concession securing a TV series?

indicators.note: to secure is to hold fast, so one piece grips another inside it

parts.note: a sop is a small concession made to placate someone
taken as written

explanation.surface: A broadcaster's grudging compromise wins a television programme.
explanation.walkthrough: A sop is a token concession offered to keep someone quiet; the single A sits inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A soap, short for soap opera, is a long-running television drama serial about everyday lives.

clue.text: French food that is to the rear of British

indicators.note: being at the rear means coming behind, so this piece is placed after the other

parts.note: Br is a standard abbreviation for British
i.e. is the Latin abbreviation id est, meaning that is

explanation.surface: Some French cuisine is said to lag behind Britain's.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue lists the second piece first and then says it goes behind the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Brie is a soft cheese originating in France, so it is an example of French food.

clue.text: Popular group, with leader away, failing to perform

indicators.note: when the leader is away the front is missing, so the opening letter is dropped

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular
a faction is a group within a larger body

explanation.surface: A successful band whose frontman has gone missing can no longer play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Popular group' reads as a pop band, but the two words are separate pieces; the group loses its first letter F.
explanation.definitionFit: Inaction is a state of not doing anything; the definition is a phrase describing that idleness, a noun idea.

clue.text: Oppose wild jumping Jack abandons

indicators.note: wild means uncontrolled and disordered, so the remaining letters are scrambled
whoever abandons a place leaves it, so that letter is removed

parts.note: taken as written
J is the card abbreviation for jack

explanation.surface: A frantic leaping Jack gives up the fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumping Jack' looks like a phrase, but Jack is the J to be taken out of the first word before the rest is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To impugn a claim is to challenge or dispute its truth, a formal synonym for opposing it.

clue.text: Former lover abandoned bottle, almost free

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is cut off

parts.note: an ex is a former partner
an empty is a drained bottle that has been discarded

explanation.surface: An old flame has left a bottle behind and is nearly at liberty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abandoned' looks like it describes the lover, but it belongs with 'bottle': an empty is a finished bottle, a noun here.
explanation.definitionFit: To be exempt is to be released from an obligation or rule, so free of it.

clue.text: Group of hunters satisfied bagging tail of grouse

indicators.note: bagging is putting into a bag, so one piece is enclosed by another

parts.note: to have met a need is to have satisfied it

indicators.note: the tail is the back end, so only the closing letter is kept

parts.note: last letter of grouse

explanation.surface: A shooting party is pleased to have bagged a grouse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bagging' fits the hunting picture perfectly but is the container signal. A meet is the gathering of riders and hounds before a hunt.
explanation.definitionFit: In fox hunting, a meet is the assembly of huntsmen and hounds, a specialist sense of the word.

clue.text: Road marker from motorway with large English letters

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's best-known motorway, with the digit read as the letter I
L is the clothing abbreviation for large
E is the standard abbreviation for English
post is the mail, letters collectively

explanation.surface: A roadside sign on a motorway bears big English lettering.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is the motorway from London to Leeds, and the digit 1 stands in for the letter I. 'Letters' is not about the sign's writing but the post.
explanation.definitionFit: A milepost is a post set beside a road showing distance in miles, so it marks the road.

clue.text: Bet political advisor will keep source of scandal in reserve

definitions.note: the answer is a verb meaning to put in reserve; the definition is the phrase it completes

parts.note: to lay a bet is to wager it

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold on to it, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: an aide is an assistant or advisor to a politician

indicators.note: a source is where something starts, so only the first letter is used

parts.note: first letter of scandal

explanation.surface: A wager that a spin doctor will hold back a juicy story for later.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is spread over the end of the clue: the answer means to keep something in reserve, with 'will keep' doing double duty as the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To lay aside something is to put it away for later use, holding it back as a store.

clue.text: Sort of comic artist is funny

indicators.note: funny can mean odd or peculiar, so the letters are put into a strange new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A kind of comedian is an artist who makes people laugh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Funny' looks like the definition of a comic, but it is the signal to rearrange the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A satirist uses mockery and ridicule to attack folly, a particular kind of humorist or comedian.

clue.text: Bored concealing power provided by working munitions

indicators.note: to conceal is to hide inside, so one piece is wrapped around another

parts.note: weary means tired and fed up, as one is when bored
P is the physics symbol for power
a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: A jaded factory worker hides the energy that drives an arms plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bored' suggests drilling a gun barrel, but it means tired; P and ON together are tucked inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Munitions are military weapons and ammunition, and weaponry is the collective term for arms.

clue.text: Wordplay is hard to beat?

parts.note: a pun is a play on words
taken as written
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: Clever verbal humour is something difficult to top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard to beat' reads as an unbeatable phrase, but it splits: hard gives H, and beat is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To beat someone can mean to hit them as a penalty, which is one way to punish them.

clue.text: Web program beginning to harm two things

parts.note: a bot is an automated program that runs on the internet

indicators.note: the beginning is the very start, so only the opening letter is used

parts.note: first letter of harm

explanation.surface: A piece of online software sets out to damage a couple of things.
explanation.walkthrough: A bot, short for robot, is software that performs automated tasks online.
explanation.definitionFit: Both refers to the pair together, each of the two items being considered at once.

clue.text: Negative comment involving the French debut for Ravel — this piece?

definitions.note: 'this' points back to the composer named in the clue

indicators.note: to involve is to include within, so other letters go inside

parts.note: a boo is a jeer of disapproval
le is French for the

indicators.note: a debut is a first appearance, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: first letter of Ravel

explanation.surface: A jeer greets the premiere of a French composer's work.
explanation.walkthrough: Ravel does double duty: its first letter goes in the jeer, and the question mark points to his most famous work.
explanation.definitionFit: Ravel's Bolero is his best-known orchestral composition, so it is the musical work the clue hints at.

clue.text: Church expert accepting new risk

parts.note: CH is the standard abbreviation for church

indicators.note: accepting something means taking it in, so a piece is placed inside another

parts.note: an ace is a highly skilled person
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A specialist in ecclesiastical matters agrees to take on a fresh gamble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Church expert' looks like one figure, a theologian, but it splits into two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To chance something is to risk it, and as nouns both mean a gamble with uncertain outcome.

clue.text: Ring Houses of Parliament initially about nothing

indicators.note: about means around, so one set of letters surrounds another
initially means at the start, so the first letter of each word is taken

parts.note: first letters of the three words
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Someone phones Westminster to begin with, about nothing at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring' suggests a phone call to Parliament, but it is the definition, a circle. The Houses of Parliament are the UK legislature at Westminster.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoop is a circular band of metal or wood, so it is a ring in shape.

clue.text: Limits or borders of European domains

indicators.note: the borders are the outer edges, so only the outside letters of each word are kept

parts.note: first and last letters of European
first and last letters of domains

explanation.surface: A question about the frontiers of European territories.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Borders' looks like a second definition alongside 'Limits', but it is the signal to take the outer letters of the next two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Ends are the furthest points of something, the boundaries beyond which it stops, as limits are.

clue.text: Liberal American backed attempt with passion

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective meaning passionate; the definition is a phrase of the same sense

indicators.note: going backward means running in the opposite direction, so the letters read right to left

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for Liberal
US stands for the United States
a try is an attempt

explanation.surface: A left-leaning American supported an effort with real fervour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backed' reads as supported, fitting the political picture, but it turns the first two pieces around.
explanation.definitionFit: Sultry describes something sensual and smouldering, suggestive of passionate desire.

clue.text: Ran round Sidney, off-balance

indicators.note: going round something means encircling it, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: to lope is to run with long easy strides
Sid is the shortened first name for Sidney, made by a deletion of its last three letters

explanation.surface: Someone ran in circles around Sidney until he was dizzy and unsteady.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ran round' looks like a single phrase, but 'round' is the container signal and 'Ran' supplies the outer word.
explanation.definitionFit: Something lopsided leans to one side because its weight is uneven, so it is unbalanced.

clue.text: Right to deploy plan

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for right
to deploy something is to put it to use

explanation.surface: Someone claims the authority to put a strategy into action.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right to deploy' reads as an entitlement, but it is a single letter followed by a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A ruse is a cunning scheme or trick, a crafty stratagem rather than a neutral plan.
